# Git for Teams {#sec-git-teams}

```{r}
#| label: git-teams-opening
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
set.seed(20261009)
n_cohort <- 2000
cohort_raw <- tibble(
  patient_id = sprintf("%04d", seq_len(n_cohort)),
  sbp = pmax(round(138 + 25 * rt(n_cohort, df = 4)), 0),
  dbp = pmax(round(80 + 20 * rt(n_cohort, df = 4)), 0),
  outcome = ifelse(runif(n_cohort) < 0.03, NA,
                   rbinom(n_cohort, 1, 0.22))
)
count_cohort <- function(...) {
  nrow(filter(cohort_raw, ..., !is.na(outcome)))
}
n_base     <- count_cohort(sbp <= 250)
n_yours    <- count_cohort(sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150)
n_hers     <- count_cohort(sbp >= 50, sbp <= 220)
n_resolved <- count_cohort(sbp >= 50, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150)
stopifnot(length(unique(c(n_yours, n_hers, n_resolved))) == 3)
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

You tighten the blood-pressure exclusions in a cohort script on
your branch, and the cohort has `r fmt(n_yours)` patients. A
colleague, on her own branch, edits the same filter for a reason of
her own, and her cohort has `r fmt(n_hers)`. Both counts are right,
both branches pass their checks, and once the two are merged the
cohort has `r fmt(n_resolved)` patients, a number neither of you
has seen and nobody has checked. Git can tell you that two people
edited the same lines; it cannot tell you what the combination
means for the analysis. This chapter covers the mechanics of
sharing a repository and the review practices that make the
combined result somebody's deliberate decision.

## Remotes, fetch, and the two shapes of history {#sec-git-teams-remotes}

The mechanics of Git are largely indifferent to the number of
people using them: the commit is still a snapshot, the branch is
still a movable pointer, and the tag is still fixed. What changes
when a second person joins is the object Git maintains. The
repository is no longer the record of what you did; it is the
record of what the team did, and the team must be able to
reconstruct the analysis from it. Three consequences organize this
chapter: two people editing one file will eventually collide
(@sec-git-teams-conflicts); the history becomes something a
colleague reads, so a careless commit message becomes a shared
cost; and a change to the analysis now arrives from someone else,
so someone must look at it before it becomes the analysis of
record (@sec-git-teams-review).

A remote is a copy of the repository somewhere else, usually on
GitHub, conventionally named `origin`. Your local repository
caches the remote's state in a *remote-tracking branch* called
`origin/main`, which is only as fresh as your last fetch.

```bash
git fetch origin        # update origin/main; touch nothing else
git status              # 'behind by 3 commits' now means something
git log --oneline main..origin/main    # what they did
git log --oneline origin/main..main    # what I did
```

Of all the network operations in Git, `git fetch` is the one that
cannot surprise you: it updates your picture of the remote and
leaves your own work untouched. Form the habit of fetching first
and looking, rather than pulling and finding out.

When you and a collaborator have both committed, the two histories
have diverged and must be reconciled, in one of two ways
(@tbl-git-teams-merge-rebase).

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `git merge origin/main` | `git rebase origin/main` |
| What it does | Creates a new commit with two parents, one from each line of work | Replays your commits, one at a time, on top of theirs |
| The history | A true record: two lines existed in parallel and were joined | Linear: reads as though you had started from their latest state |
| Use it for | Integrating a completed branch | Your own unpushed work |
| Never | (no restriction) | On commits that someone else has pulled |

: The two shapes of history. {#tbl-git-teams-merge-rebase}

`git pull` is a fetch followed by one of these, chosen by
configuration, which is exactly the ambiguity that makes it a poor
thing to type without thinking. Configure it explicitly once:

```bash
git config --global pull.rebase true    # or false, but choose
```

For a small analysis team, rebase on pull for your own unpushed
work and merge for integrating a completed branch is a workable
default: your local history stays clean, and the integration of a
finished piece of work is recorded as the event it was. The one
absolute rule is the one every Git tutorial states and every team
eventually violates: **never rebase commits that someone else has
pulled.** Rewriting shared history forces everyone downstream to
reconcile a history that no longer matches theirs, and the
recovery is tedious.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Recovering a shared branch is where a model's first suggestion can
destroy a colleague's work. State the situation and forbid the
rewrite.

> **Context.** I pushed a commit to the shared branch `main` that
> [deleted `R/sensitivity.R` by mistake], and my colleague may
> already have pulled it. Below are `git status`,
> `git log --oneline --graph -10`, and the output of
> `git log --oneline origin/main..main` and
> `git log --oneline main..origin/main` after a fetch.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not propose `git push --force`, a
> `git reset` of any pushed commit, or anything else that rewrites
> history on the remote. Prefer `git revert`. If you believe a
> rewrite is unavoidable, say why, and use `--force-with-lease`.
>
> **Criteria.** After your commands, `git log origin/main` still
> contains every commit it contained before, plus new ones, and
> `git status` reports that `main` is up to date with
> `origin/main`. Explain each command before I run it.

*Failure mode.* The suggestion contains `git push --force`. On a
shared branch a force push discards commits that your colleagues
may already have pulled, and it is the one operation in this
chapter that can lose another person's work.
`git push --force-with-lease` is the safer form, because it refuses
when the remote has moved since you last fetched (an IDE, or
integrated development environment, that fetches in the background can defeat that check). Better still is
`git revert`, which undoes a commit by adding a new one and
rewrites nothing. *Check.* Before any history-altering command on
a shared branch, ask a simpler question: has anyone else pulled
this? If the answer is yes or unknown, revert rather than rewrite,
and compare `git log --oneline origin/main` before and after. Logs
hold commit messages and file names, not data, so they may go to
any approved tool; read the messages for identifiers first
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `git status` says your branch is up to date with
`origin/main`. Does that mean nobody has pushed since you started
work?

**Answer.** No. `git status` compares your branch with your cached
copy of the remote, which changes only when you fetch. If you have
not fetched since this morning, 'up to date' means up to date with
this morning. `git fetch` first, then `git status`; or ask the
server directly with `git ls-remote origin main`.
:::

## Feature branches and pull requests {#sec-git-teams-prs}

The workflow that scales from two statisticians to twenty is the
one used across open-source software. @fig-git-pr shows its shape.
Work happens on a short-lived branch named for what it does. When
it is ready, it is proposed for inclusion through a pull request,
which is a request that someone else look at it. CI (continuous
integration, @sec-ci) runs against the proposed merge. A human
reviews. Only then does it join the analysis of record.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-git-pr
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart of the feature-branch workflow. Create a
%%|   feature branch, commit and push, open a pull request, then CI
%%|   checks and colleague review. A decision node asks whether both
%%|   pass: if no, the loop returns to commit and push; if yes, the
%%|   branch merges to main."
%%| fig-cap: "The feature-branch workflow. Work never lands on `main`
%%|   directly: it arrives through a pull request that CI has checked
%%|   and a colleague has read. The branch is short-lived and is
%%|   deleted once merged."
flowchart TD
  A["create feature branch"] --> B["commit, push"]
  B --> C["open pull request"]
  C --> D["CI checks and colleague review"]
  D --> E{"both pass?"}
  E -->|"no"| B
  E -->|"yes"| F["merge to main"]
```

In commands:

```bash
# 1. branch from the current main
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c sensitivity-mnar

# 2. work, commit, push the branch
git add R/sensitivity.R
git commit -m "Add delta-adjustment sensitivity under MNAR"
git push -u origin sensitivity-mnar

# 3. open the pull request
gh pr create --fill --reviewer colleague-username

# 4. after review and a green check
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch
```

The `--squash` flag collapses the branch's commits into one on
`main`. For an analysis repository this is usually right: the
fifteen commits of a working afternoon ('fix typo', 'actually fix
typo') are noise, and what `main` should record is the one logical
change. Reserve a true merge for branches whose internal commits
are each meaningful.

Three properties of the workflow are the reasons to adopt it
rather than pushing to `main` and hoping. **Nothing unreviewed
becomes the analysis**: the pull request is a gate that a human
must open. **CI checks the proposal, not the aftermath**: the
workflow of @sec-ci, which restores `renv`, runs the tests, and
renders the report, answers 'does this change break the analysis'
before the change lands. **The branch is a unit of thought**: six
months later, the pull request that merged `sensitivity-mnar` is a
small, self-contained record of what was added, why, and what the
reviewer asked, the best record of an analytic decision the
tooling will ever give you for free.

### Protecting `main`

The `main` branch is the version of the analysis you would defend,
and anything that has not been reviewed and has not passed CI is
not that. The workflow is a convention until the repository
enforces it.
On GitHub, in the repository's settings, add a branch
protection rule or a ruleset for `main` that requires a pull
request before merging, requires the status check from @sec-ci
to pass, and forbids force pushes. Three caveats, as of this
writing (GitHub moves these settings between plans and pages
from time to time): repository administrators can bypass a
rule unless you also choose the option that applies it to them;
on GitHub's free plan, rules are enforced on public
repositories but not on private ones, which need a paid or
organization plan; and the newer rulesets page offers the same
protections under different names. On a team of one this is
unnecessary; on a team of two it is the cheapest insurance
available, because the failure it
prevents (a hurried Friday push straight to `main` that breaks
the render and is discovered on Monday) is the one that
actually happens.

### Exercises

1. In a repository of your own that GitHub enforces rules on (a
   public one, or a private one on a paid or organization plan),
   protect `main`: require a pull request, require a status check,
   forbid force pushes, and apply the rule to administrators.
   Then try to push a commit directly to `main`. What happens?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The push is rejected: Git prints the remote's error, which names
the protected branch and the rule that blocked it, and `main` on
GitHub is unchanged (`git ls-remote origin main` still prints the
old hash). If the push succeeds, one of the caveats above applies:
the rule exempts administrators, or the plan does not enforce rules
on a private repository. Push the commit to a branch instead and
open a pull request; `gh pr checks` then shows the required status
check.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You and one colleague, who is careful and whom you
trust, are the only contributors. Why not simply agree to be
careful and push to `main`?

**Answer.** Because the protection is not against carelessness, it
is against the absence of a second reader. Pushing to `main` means
the analysis of record changed and nobody looked. The pull request
costs about ninety seconds and buys three things you cannot get
otherwise: a second pair of eyes on a statistical change, a CI run
against the proposed state rather than the merged one, and a
durable written record of why the change was made, attached to the
change itself. The 'we are careful' argument also fails for a
structural reason: what you are guarding against is not your
colleague's carelessness, nor your own, but the interaction of two
correct changes that are wrong together. No individual can catch
that by being careful alone.
:::

## Merge conflicts {#sec-git-teams-conflicts}

A conflict occurs when two commits change the same region of the
same file and Git, unable to decide which of the two changes to
keep, declines to guess. It writes markers into the file and
stops. Suppose that you and a colleague have each edited the same
filter in a cohort-construction script, in which `sbp` and `dbp`
are systolic and diastolic blood pressure:

```r
analytic <- visits |>
  filter(
<<<<<<< HEAD
    sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150,
=======
    sbp >= 50, sbp <= 220,
>>>>>>> origin/main
    !is.na(outcome)
  )
```

The region above `=======` is what you have; the region below is
what arrived. The marker `>>>>>>>` names its source. Your job is to
edit the file so that it says what the analysis should say, and to
delete all three marker lines.

**A merge conflict is a disagreement about the analysis, not about
the text.** The tooling invites you to pick a winner; read the
conflict instead as two statements about the analysis. Yours drops
implausibly high systolic and diastolic pressures; theirs adds a
lower bound on systolic pressure and tightens its upper bound from
250 to 220. Two of these three changes are not alternatives at
all: the diastolic ceiling and the systolic floor are halves of a
single decision that the two of you reached independently, and
both belong in the result. The third, the systolic ceiling, is a
genuine disagreement that no merge can settle. The resolution that
preserves both intents, keeping the ceiling the analysis plan
specifies (here 250) until the disagreement is resolved, is the
following:

```r
analytic <- visits |>
  filter(
    sbp >= 50, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150,
    !is.na(outcome)
  )
```

It matches neither side, which is the sign that it was written
rather than chosen. Send a message to your colleague asking why
220, because one of you has a reason and the other should hear it.
The conflict surfaced a substantive disagreement about an
exclusion criterion that would otherwise have been settled
silently by whoever pushed last. That is the conflict doing its
job.

### What the resolution does to the cohort

The cohort in this chapter is synthetic: `r fmt(n_cohort)` patients
generated in the chapter's source with a fixed seed, some with
implausible pressures and some with a missing outcome. Counting it
under each version of the filter shows why the merged count needs
its own check.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-git-teams-conflict-counts
#| tbl-cap: "The cohort under each version of the filter. The
#|   resolved filter matches neither branch, so neither branch's
#|   count describes the merged analysis."
library(dplyr)

with_outcome <- filter(cohort_raw, !is.na(outcome))
tibble(
  version = c("main before either branch", "Your branch",
              "Her branch", "Resolved"),
  filter = c("sbp <= 250", "sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150",
             "sbp >= 50, sbp <= 220",
             "sbp >= 50, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150"),
  patients = c(
    nrow(filter(with_outcome, sbp <= 250)),
    nrow(filter(with_outcome, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150)),
    nrow(filter(with_outcome, sbp >= 50, sbp <= 220)),
    nrow(filter(with_outcome, sbp >= 50, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150))
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Relative to your branch, the resolution loses the patients below
the systolic floor. Relative to hers, it gains those with systolic
pressure from 221 to 250 and a diastolic pressure within the
ceiling, and loses those she kept whose diastolic pressure exceeds
150. You should be able to account for both differences before you
commit the resolution.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before concluding a merge, confirm that no markers remain and that
the merged analysis gives the count you can explain:

```bash
git grep -n -e '<<<<<<<' -e '>>>>>>>'   # no output: no markers
Rscript -e 'source("R/cohort.R"); nrow(analytic)'
```

Compare the count with both branches' counts and account for each
difference, as above. A count that equals one side's exactly after
a conflict in a filter usually means that side was chosen, not
merged.
:::

The mechanics around the edit:

```bash
git status                    # which files are conflicted
# ... edit each file, remove all markers ...
git add R/cohort.R            # mark this file resolved
git commit                    # conclude the merge

git merge --abort             # or: back out, think, try again
```

`git merge --abort` returns you to the state before the merge
began and is the right move whenever the conflict is larger than
you expected. There is no penalty for backing out and approaching
it again with the diff in front of you.

### Conflicts in generated files

A conflict in a hand-written R script is a genuine disagreement and
deserves a human. A conflict in a file that a program writes is
different: resolve it by regenerating the file, never by editing
it. A conflict in `renv.lock` is a real dependency disagreement
wearing the costume of a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) merge
failure: decide which
dependency state you want, take that side's lockfile, and rebuild
from it with `renv::restore()`, reinstall anything of yours that is
genuinely still needed, and `renv::snapshot()` (@sec-renv explains
the three verbs).

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Under a rebase, `--theirs` is your own work.** Taking one side
of a conflicted file wholesale is usually written
`git checkout --theirs <file>`. The meaning of `--theirs` depends
on the operation. During a merge it is the branch you are merging
in (here `origin/main`). During a rebase, including the rebase that
`git pull` performs once `pull.rebase` is `true` as recommended
above, the roles are reversed: `--ours` is the upstream you are
replaying onto and `--theirs` is your own commit. The command
succeeds either way and the file looks plausible either way. To
avoid guessing, name the commit instead of the side:
`git checkout origin/main -- renv.lock` takes the version on
`origin/main` in either case.
:::

### The conflicts that should never happen

Most conflicts a research team experiences are self-inflicted,
caused by committing files that are outputs rather than sources. A
rendered `paper.html`, a `_freeze/` cache, a `figures/*.png`, an
`.Rproj.user/` directory: every one of these changes on every
render, on every machine, and every one of them will conflict,
meaninglessly, forever. The remedy is a `.gitignore` that keeps
them out of the repository:

```
# outputs and caches
*.html
*.pdf
/_book/
/figures/
.Rproj.user/
.Rhistory
.RData

# renv library (the lockfile is committed; the library is not)
renv/library/
renv/staging/
```

@sec-quarto argues for committing `_freeze/` so that collaborators
and CI need not re-run expensive chunks. That argument stands, and
it is in genuine tension with this one. Resolve it by deciding as a
team: either commit `_freeze/` and accept that the person who
renders last regenerates it (and resolve any conflict in it by
regenerating, per the rule above), or leave it out and let CI bear
the cost. Both are defensible. Not deciding is what produces the
weekly conflict nobody understands.

Two kinds of file repay a `.gitattributes` entry, which tells Git
how to treat them:

```
*.rds binary
*.qmd text eol=lf
```

You may see `renv.lock merge=ours` recommended for the
lockfile. Leave it out. Git defines no `ours` merge driver, so
on its own the line does nothing and the lockfile still
conflicts; once someone also runs
`git config merge.ours.driver true`, Git silently keeps your
lockfile and discards your collaborator's on every merge, with
no conflict to prompt the regeneration described above. That is
picking a side wholesale, without the decision.

The line-ending declaration matters more than it looks: a team
that mixes Windows and macOS machines without it will eventually
produce a diff in which every line of a file has changed, and no
review is possible through that noise (@sec-shell shows what a
carriage return looks like at the byte level).

### Exercises

2. Plant the chapter's conflict in a throwaway repository. In an
   empty directory, run the commands below, which define a small
   function that rewrites `R/cohort.R` with a given filter line.
   Then, on a branch `dbp-ceiling`, call
   `write_cohort 'sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150,'` and commit; return to
   `main`, create a branch `sbp-range`, call
   `write_cohort 'sbp >= 50, sbp <= 220,'` and commit; merge
   `sbp-range` into `main`; switch to `dbp-ceiling` and run
   `git merge main`. (SAP, in the first commit message, is the
   statistical analysis plan.) What does the merge print, what does
   `git status --short` show, and what does `Rscript R/cohort.R`
   print on each branch and after you resolve the conflict as this
   section does?

```bash
git init -b main
printf '%s\n' 'id,sbp,dbp,outcome' '1,120,80,0' '2,135,85,1' \
  '3,140,90,0' '4,260,100,1' '5,230,95,0' '6,240,160,1' \
  '7,45,30,0' '8,150,155,0' '9,125,82,' '10,110,70,1' \
  '11,225,100,0' > visits.csv
mkdir R
write_cohort() {
  printf '%s\n' 'suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))' \
    'visits <- read.csv("visits.csv")' \
    'analytic <- visits |>' '  filter(' "    $1" \
    '    !is.na(outcome)' '  )' 'nrow(analytic)' > R/cohort.R
}
write_cohort 'sbp <= 250,'
git add .
git commit -m 'Build cohort with the SAP exclusions'
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The merge of `sbp-range` into `main` is a fast-forward. The merge
of `main` into `dbp-ceiling` prints:

```
Auto-merging R/cohort.R
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in R/cohort.R
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

`git status --short` prints `UU R/cohort.R`, and the file holds the
conflict shown at the start of this section, with `>>>>>>> main` as
the last marker. Resolve it with
`write_cohort 'sbp >= 50, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150,'`, then
`git add R/cohort.R` and `git commit --no-edit`. The counts, which
`Rscript R/cohort.R` prints as `[1] 9` and so on, are computed here
from the same eleven rows:

```{r}
#| label: soln-05b-2
toy <- read.csv(text = paste(
  "id,sbp,dbp,outcome", "1,120,80,0", "2,135,85,1", "3,140,90,0",
  "4,260,100,1", "5,230,95,0", "6,240,160,1", "7,45,30,0",
  "8,150,155,0", "9,125,82,", "10,110,70,1", "11,225,100,0",
  sep = "\n"))
c(main_before  = nrow(filter(toy, sbp <= 250, !is.na(outcome))),
  dbp_ceiling  = nrow(filter(toy, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150,
                             !is.na(outcome))),
  sbp_range    = nrow(filter(toy, sbp >= 50, sbp <= 220,
                             !is.na(outcome))),
  resolved     = nrow(filter(toy, sbp >= 50, sbp <= 250, dbp <= 150,
                             !is.na(outcome))))
```

Relative to `dbp-ceiling`, the resolution loses patient 7 (systolic
45); relative to `sbp-range`, it gains patients 5 and 11 (systolic
230 and 225) and loses patient 8 (diastolic 155). `git log --oneline
--graph` then shows the two lines of work meeting at
`Merge branch 'main' into dbp-ceiling`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Two statisticians edit the cleaning script. One
tightens the plausible blood-pressure range; the other adds an
exclusion for missing outcomes, in a different part of the file.
Git merges both without a conflict. Is that the right outcome?

**Answer.** Git did the right thing. Whether the *analysis* is
right is a question Git cannot reach, and this is the limit of what
version control buys a team. A merge conflict is a textual
condition: two branches changed overlapping lines. These edits did
not overlap, so the merge is clean and both changes are now in
effect together, which is very likely what nobody tested. The
analytic cohort is now smaller than either statistician intended,
and each will assume the count they saw on their own branch.

This is the semantic-conflict case, and it is the argument for the
pull request rather than for Git. A human reading the diff asks
what the combined effect on the cohort is; a merge algorithm
cannot. It is also the argument for the integration test of
@sec-testing: an assertion on the final row count, or on the
number of exclusions at each step, fails on the merged code even
though neither change failed alone. State the row count in the pull
request description: two pull requests that each say 'n drops from
500 to 480' should make a reviewer ask what happens when both land.
:::

## Reviewing an analysis diff {#sec-git-teams-review}

A software engineer reviewing a diff asks whether it is correct,
tested, and clear. A statistician reviewing an analysis diff asks
those questions and then the ones that matter more, which a green
test suite does not answer. The review is where the statistical
judgment of @sec-team-science meets the infrastructure of this
chapter, and it is the highest-value thing a second pair of eyes
does on a research compendium. @tbl-git-teams-review is the
checklist, in rough order of how often each question catches
something.

| Question | Why it matters | In the diff, look for |
|---|---|---|
| Did the denominator change? | A new filter anywhere upstream changes the sample size of everything downstream | A new or edited `filter()`: how many rows does it remove, is that number reported, and does the analysis plan sanction the exclusion? |
| Did the join cardinality change? | A join can silently multiply or drop rows (@sec-joins) | A new or changed join without a `relationship` argument, which is incomplete |
| Is the seed still set, and in the same place? | Moving `set.seed()`, or adding a random step above it, changes every random draw downstream; the diff will not say so | A moved `set.seed()`, or a new `sample()`, `rnorm()`, or resampling call above it |
| Is this analysis pre-specified? | A new model, covariate, or subgroup is either in the analysis plan (@sec-analysis-plan) or exploratory, and the code should say which | New terms in a model formula, new subgroup filters |
| Are the numbers in the prose still computed? | A changed model with a typed estimate in the text makes the manuscript wrong (@sec-quarto) | A changed model and an unchanged number in a `.qmd` |
| Does the test suite exercise the change? | A new branch in the cleaning logic with no test will break silently later (@sec-testing) | New `if` or `case_when()` branches with no new test |

: The analysis-diff review checklist. {#tbl-git-teams-review}

Leave the review as comments on the pull request, on the specific
lines. The conversation is then attached to the change for good,
which is worth more than the same conversation held at a desk.

### Exercises

3. Review this diff against @tbl-git-teams-review. Which checklist
   questions does it raise, and is there one change that looks
   risky but is not?

```diff
--- a/R/analysis.R
+++ b/R/analysis.R
@@ -1,13 +1,15 @@
 library(dplyr)
-set.seed(20260423)

 cohort <- readr::read_csv("data/derived/cohort.csv") |>
-  filter(!is.na(outcome))
+  filter(!is.na(outcome), age >= 18)
+
+cohort <- cohort |>
+  left_join(labs_baseline, by = "patient_id")

+set.seed(20260423)
 boot <- replicate(2000, {
-  fit <- glm(outcome ~ arm, family = binomial,
+  fit <- glm(outcome ~ arm + egfr, family = binomial,
              data = slice_sample(cohort, prop = 1, replace = TRUE))
   coef(fit)[["armHome health"]]
 })
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Three questions apply. *Denominator*: `age >= 18` is a new
exclusion; ask how many rows it removes, whether the number is
reported, and whether the analysis plan sanctions it (in a trial
that enrolled only adults it should remove none, and a non-zero
count is itself a finding). *Join cardinality*: the `left_join()`
to `labs_baseline` has no `relationship` argument; if a patient has
two baseline lab rows, the cohort multiplies, and every bootstrap
sample with it. Ask for `relationship = "many-to-one"` and a row
count before and after. *Pre-specification*: `egfr` is a new
covariate in the primary model; it is either in the plan or it is
an exploratory analysis, and the code should say which.

The moved `set.seed()` looks risky and is not, here: nothing
between its old and new positions draws a random number (reading a
file, filtering, and joining do not), so the bootstrap draws are
unchanged. Verify rather than assume: run the old and new versions
on the same data with the join and filter removed, and compare the
first few bootstrap estimates. A review that flags everything
unusual teaches the author to ignore the review; say which changes
matter and why.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A pull request changes only `R/models.R`, its tests
pass, and the diff is small and idiomatic. What is the one
question from @tbl-git-teams-review that a reviewer who knows no
statistics would never ask?

**Answer.** Whether the analysis is pre-specified. Everything else
on the list a careful engineer might stumble on (a changed row
count, a new join, a moved seed), but whether a new covariate or
subgroup appears in the analysis plan can be answered only by
someone who has read the plan and knows why it matters. That is
the question a statistician reviewer exists to ask.
:::

## Attribution: blame and bisect {#sec-git-teams-bisect}

When a number changes and nobody knows why, two commands answer
the question. `git blame` reports, for every line of a file, the
commit that last changed it:

```bash
git blame -L 40,60 R/cohort.R
```

The `-L` flag restricts the output to a line range, which is
almost always what you want. The command is named unfortunately;
its use is archaeological rather than accusatory. The commit hash
it reports leads to the message, which leads (if the advice of
@sec-git-solo about messages that explain why was followed) to the
reason.

`git bisect` finds the commit that changed a result, by binary
search over the history. You name a commit where the result was
right and one where it was wrong, and it checks out the midpoint
and asks you:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current state is wrong
git bisect good v1.0-submitted # this tag was right
# Git checks out a midpoint; you re-run and judge:
git bisect good                # or: git bisect bad
# ... repeat about log2(n) times ...
# Git names the first bad commit.
git bisect reset
```

Over a hundred commits this converges in about seven steps. It can
be automated, which is where it becomes genuinely useful on an
analysis repository:

```bash
git bisect run Rscript -e 'stopifnot(abs(get_estimate() - 0.62) < 0.01)'
```

Git runs the command at each midpoint and uses its exit status to
decide. The prerequisite is atomic commits (@sec-git-solo): bisect
over a history of 'Tuesday's work' commits will correctly identify
the day the result changed and tell you nothing useful about why.

### Exercises

4. In a new throwaway repository, copy in the `visits.csv` from
   Exercise 2 and commit `R/estimate.R`, which computes the event
   rate among patients with `sbp <= 250`; tag that commit
   `v1.0-submitted`. Then make four more commits: add a README;
   change the threshold to `sbp <= 230` with the message 'Tidy the
   exclusion code'; extend the README; add a comment to
   `R/estimate.R`. Use `git bisect run` with a one-line assertion
   to find the commit that changed the estimate. How many commits
   does Git test, and what does it print?

```bash
printf '%s\n' 'visits <- read.csv("visits.csv")' \
  'keep <- visits$sbp <= 250 & !is.na(visits$outcome)' \
  'est <- mean(visits$outcome[keep])' > R/estimate.R
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The estimate at the tag and after the change, from the same rows:

```{r}
#| label: soln-05b-4
round(c(
  submitted = mean(toy$outcome[toy$sbp <= 250 & !is.na(toy$outcome)]),
  after     = mean(toy$outcome[toy$sbp <= 230 & !is.na(toy$outcome)])
), 3)
```

The assertion is therefore
`git bisect run Rscript -e 'source("R/estimate.R"); stopifnot(round(est, 3) == 0.333)'`,
after `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, and
`git bisect good v1.0-submitted`. With four commits after the
tag, Git tests two of them and prints (your hash differs):

```
f6b1f7c2f0b0ce6fd12b33e16905f5e688dabe96 is the first 'bad' commit
commit f6b1f7c2f0b0ce6fd12b33e16905f5e688dabe96
Author: Reader <reader@example.com>

    Tidy the exclusion code
```

followed by the commit's file summary and `bisect found first 'bad'
commit`. Run `git bisect reset` to return to `main`. The message
'Tidy the exclusion code' is the lesson: a commit described as a
refactor changed a reported number, and only a test of the number
found it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `git bisect run` reports that a merge commit is the
first bad commit, and each of the two branches it joined is good on
its own. What happened?

**Answer.** A semantic conflict: two changes, each correct alone,
are wrong together, as in the clean merge of the Check in
@sec-git-teams-conflicts. Bisect has located the moment the
combination first existed, which is the right answer; the fix is a
decision about how the two changes should combine, made with both
authors, not a revert of either.
:::

## Worked example: two statisticians, one compendium {#sec-git-teams-worked}

The scenario: you and a colleague are analyzing the readmissions
cohort of @tbl-git-teams-conflict-counts. You take the primary
model; she takes the missing-data sensitivity analysis. Both of you
touch the cohort-construction script.

```bash
# Monday. Both of you start from the same main.
git switch main && git pull

# You branch for the primary model.
git switch -c primary-model
# (edit R/model.R; also tighten an exclusion in R/cohort.R)
git add R/model.R R/cohort.R
git commit -m "Fit primary logistic model; exclude SBP > 250, DBP > 150"
git push -u origin primary-model
gh pr create --fill --reviewer colleague
```

Meanwhile she has branched `mnar-sensitivity` from the same `main`,
and has also edited `R/cohort.R`, adding a lower bound on systolic
pressure and lowering its ceiling to 220. Her pull request is
reviewed and merged first. Yours is now out of date, and GitHub
says so.

```bash
# Bring main into your branch and deal with the conflict.
git switch primary-model
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in R/cohort.R
```

You open `R/cohort.R`, find the conflict shown in
@sec-git-teams-conflicts, and recognize that two of the three edits
are complementary rather than competing. You keep her systolic
floor and your diastolic ceiling, keep the plan's systolic ceiling
of 250, and leave a comment on her merged pull request asking where
220 came from.

```bash
git add R/cohort.R
git commit                    # concludes the merge
git push
```

CI re-runs against the updated branch. It fails: the combined
cohort now has `r fmt(n_resolved)` rows, and a test in
`inst/tinytest/test-cohort.R`, written on your branch, asserted
`r fmt(n_yours)`. The test is doing its job. You account for the
difference (@tbl-git-teams-conflict-counts), update the assertion,
note the new denominator in the manuscript, and push again. The
check goes green, your colleague reviews the diff, asks whether the
exclusion is in the analysis plan (it is, as an amendment, tagged
before unblinding), and merges.

```bash
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch
git switch main && git pull
```

The history of `main` now contains two squashed commits, each with
a pull request behind it recording what changed, why, and what the
reviewer asked. Six months later a reviewer asks why the
denominator is `r fmt(n_resolved)` and not the `r fmt(n_base)` in
the protocol's original exclusions. The answer takes ninety seconds
to find.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
After the merge lands, confirm that `main` is what you reviewed and
that the count on `main` is the one the manuscript reports:

```bash
git switch main && git pull
git log --oneline --graph -5
Rscript -e 'source("R/cohort.R"); nrow(analytic)'
```

The log shows the two squashed commits, one per pull request, and
the count is `r fmt(n_resolved)`. A different count means something
landed on `main` that the review did not see.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the worked example, why did the failing CI check
help rather than hinder?

**Answer.** Because it turned the merged count, which neither
analyst had seen, into a decision someone had to make. Without the
assertion, the merge would have changed the denominator silently,
and the manuscript would have reported your branch's number for an
analysis that no longer produced it. Updating the assertion is
correct only after the difference is explained, which is why the
example accounts for it before pushing again.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** Nothing lands on
   `main` unreviewed: feature branch, pull request, green check,
   human reader, with branch protection to make the convention
   real.
2. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** Resolve conflicts by intent, not by side, and
   explain the merged row count before you commit it; regenerate,
   never edit, a generated file.
3. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** Review the analysis, not
   only the code: denominators, joins, seeds, pre-specification,
   and the numbers in the prose.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-solo).* Play both analysts without
   GitHub. Create a bare repository to stand in for the remote
   (`git init --bare -b main shared.git`), clone it twice (`you`
   and `colleague`), and from `you` commit and push a README. In
   `colleague`, pull, append the line `Analysis plan: SAP v1.0` to
   the README, commit, and push. In `you`, append
   `Data: HF-HOME synthetic` to the README, commit, and push. What
   does the push print? Fetch, look, merge, and resolve so that
   both lines survive.
6. *On your own work (no key).* Audit the `.gitignore` of an
   existing project of yours. List every tracked file that is a
   build product rather than a source, remove each from tracking
   with `git rm --cached`, and confirm that the analysis still
   rebuilds from what remains.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Your push is rejected, because the remote has a commit you do not:

```
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to '.../shared.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally.
```

After `git fetch`, `git status` reports
`Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have 1 and 1
different commits each, respectively`, and
`git log --oneline main..origin/main` lists your colleague's
commit. `git merge origin/main` stops with
`CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md`, because both of
you appended at the same place. Keep both lines, delete the
markers, `git add README.md`, `git commit --no-edit`, and push,
which now succeeds. In `colleague`, `git pull` brings in the merge.
The rejected push is Git protecting your colleague's work; the
fetch-and-look step is the habit of @sec-git-teams-remotes.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| See what the team did, safely | `git fetch origin`; `git log --oneline main..origin/main` |
| Make `git pull` unambiguous | `git config --global pull.rebase true` |
| Start a piece of work | `git switch -c <branch>`; `git push -u origin <branch>` |
| Propose and merge it | `gh pr create --fill --reviewer <name>`; `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch` |
| Back out of a merge | `git merge --abort` |
| Find leftover markers | `git grep -n -e '<<<<<<<' -e '>>>>>>>'` |
| Take one commit's version of a file | `git checkout origin/main -- <file>` (not `--theirs`) |
| Undo a pushed commit | `git revert <hash>` (never `push --force` on a shared branch) |
| Who last changed these lines | `git blame -L 40,60 <file>` |
| Find the commit that changed a result | `git bisect start`; `git bisect bad`; `git bisect good <tag>`; `git bisect run <cmd>` |
| Review an analysis diff | @tbl-git-teams-review |

: Git for teams at a glance. {#tbl-git-teams-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@bryan2019happygit], the standard reference for Git in R
  workflows, whose chapters on collaboration cover the same ground
  from a different angle.
- [@chacon2014progit], chapters 3 and 5, the canonical treatment
  of branching and distributed workflows.
- [@slade2023team] on team science, for the social half of the
  problem this chapter treats mechanically.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-05b}

1. `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by either `git merge` or
   `git rebase`, depending on configuration. Fetching updates
   your picture of the remote (`origin/main`) and changes
   nothing else. The reconciliation then takes one of two
   shapes: a merge creates a commit with two parents,
   preserving the fact that the two lines of work were
   parallel; a rebase replays your two commits on top of their
   three, producing a linear history that reads as though you
   had started from their latest state. Configure
   `pull.rebase` explicitly so that `git pull` stops being
   ambiguous, and never rebase commits that someone else has
   already pulled.
2. A merge conflict occurs when two commits change the same
   region of the same file and Git cannot determine which
   change to keep, so it writes both into the file between
   `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers and stops. In
   analysis code, 'take mine' or 'take theirs' is almost
   always wrong because each side usually encodes a deliberate
   analytic decision (one collaborator added a lower bound on
   an exclusion criterion; the other tightened the upper
   bound). The correct resolution preserves both intents, and
   the conflict has done something valuable by surfacing a
   substantive disagreement that a silent last-push-wins would
   have buried. The exception is a conflict in a generated
   file (`renv.lock`, a rendered document, a cache), which is
   resolved by regenerating the file rather than editing it.
3. Because the protection a pull request provides is not
   against untrustworthiness, it is against the absence of a
   second reader. It buys three things that trust does not: a
   second pair of eyes on a statistical change before it
   becomes the analysis of record, a CI run against the
   proposed state rather than after the fact, and a durable
   written record of the reasoning attached to the change
   itself. It also catches the one failure mode no amount of
   individual care can prevent: two changes that are each
   correct in isolation and wrong in combination.
